content:
### GENESIS: Plan the world, then build its opening room

First design a small connected world (3 to 6 rooms) and record the whole plan through update_world: each room's number, a short title, a one-line brief of what happens there, and its named exits to other room numbers. Room 1 is the opening room unless the brief says otherwise. Record the facts and quests the brief implies too — the plan tells every later room-authoring turn what to build. The player sees this plan on the world map as it lands and can edit it; keep the planned room numbers, titles and exits unless the map says otherwise. inspect_world_bible shows what is already recorded; read_authoring_guide has reference material if you need it.

Then author ONLY the opening room (picture 1 and logic 1 unless the brief specifies an intro/cutscene) and its required views, actors and vocabulary. DO NOT author Room 2 or subsequent rooms during Genesis. When the player walks through an exit into an unbuilt room, the engine pauses gameplay and prompts you to author that specific room just-in-time.

The supplied base template is a recommended starting point, not a requirement: use it when it fits, or extend or replace any of it to serve the brief. Its ordinary logic 0 builds the menu bar, binds the classic keys, dispatches call.v(v0) to the current room each cycle and answers unhandled input. Logic 255 and sound 255 supply a death sequence reached with call(255). Read their sources before changing them and coordinate affected room calls, state and keys. If you keep the parser fallback, set f4 after your own reply to a parsed line without a said() match.

The brief decides the shape. A plain start in room 1 is one shape; a title card, a text-screen intro paced by counters and skippable with have.key, an opening cutscene, a cursor-driven screen or something the brief invents are others. Consult read_authoring_guide only if you need reference patterns for cutscenes or interfaces.

Unless the brief specifically calls for a single-room game, design the opening room with one or more natural exits (walking edges, paths, doorways or passages) leading into the wider world. Exits simply call new.room(targetRoom). Any target room not yet authored will prompt a new room turn when the player crosses that boundary.

Deliver the opening room as a fully playable and solvable section. If the room contains puzzles or obstacles gating progress, make them completely solvable within this room and test them with write_game_tests.

Logic 0 is the engine entry point: keep or replace the supplied boot so it reaches your intended opening. Call handover only after the real boot has reached a screen the player can act on (it boots the world, dismisses windows and key waits like a player, runs every stored game test, and fails on a black screen, a missing resource or an ego placed off walkable ground; an opening without the parser or without a visible ego is fine). Inspect the picture and playtest a representative command and exit before finishing.

Write clean, unmannered prose. Say what you mean directly; avoid manufactured aphorisms, mirrored clauses, or forced metaphors. Keep narration strictly diegetic: never break the fourth wall (do not mention "this opening", "chapters", "next part of the story", or "demo"). NEVER print score awards like "(+10)" in messages; award points to variable 3 (addn(v3, points)), which the engine status line displays.

A room logic usually initializes on isset(f5): draw and show the picture, animate.obj(o0) and position and draw ego, set the horizon, accept.input(), describe the room; the rest of it handles actions and exits. For every puzzle you author, store at least one game test for it with write_game_tests and iterate with run_game_tests — handover runs every stored test before it may pass; a puzzle without a passing test is not done. Consult read_authoring_guide only if you need reference patterns for cutscenes or interfaces.

name: badge-of-millhaven
description: A rookie patrol officer learns that in Millhaven, procedure is the only weapon that never jams.
---

# Badge of Millhaven

## Premise

You are **Officer Dana Reyes**, first week on the **Millhaven** police force.
A delivery driver's story doesn't fit the pharmacy break-in. Follow the evidence
to a warehouse on Pier Road, make the arrest and bring back a case that sticks.

## Tone

A small-town police procedural with humor from paperwork and a sergeant who
has seen everything twice. Listening and connecting evidence win the day. PG-13.

## Art direction

Red brick, blue-and-white patrol cars and greenish office lights. Quiet streets,
readable shopfronts, an occasional blink from the radio.

## Protagonist

Dana wears a navy uniform, cap and duty belt. Alert, composed and recognisable
from every direction. Travel between locations is simple.

## Starting room

**The precinct front desk.** Dana has a badge and radio. Sergeant Prakash
has the assignment; the board keeps its details handy. Start with a conversation
and a useful lead.

## Lexicon

- Verbs: look, talk, read, take/get, show, check, radio/call, photograph
- Nouns: badge, driver, pharmacy, bottle, ledger, warehouse, suspect, report

## Point table (max 215)

Build a fair investigation around these milestones. Invent the evidence
and connections; award each achievement once.

| Points | Milestone                                                 |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| 10     | Receive the assignment.                                   |
| 25     | Check the delivery driver's story and find a discrepancy. |
| 30     | Document the pharmacy break-in and collect evidence.      |
| 40     | Connect the records and witness account to the warehouse. |
| 60     | Call backup and make an arrest supported by the evidence. |
| 50     | File the complete case and finish Dana's first shift.     |

## Beats

1. A small district: precinct, records office, street, pharmacy and warehouse.
   New evidence gives Dana reasons to revisit familiar people.
2. Build toward the warehouse confrontation, then bring the story back to
   Prakash's desk. Let Dana ask for reminders and correct incomplete paperwork.

## NPC seeds

- **Sergeant Prakash** — has a tray for forms completed in the wrong tray
- **Officer Bud Bukowski** — partner, talks too much, brave when it counts
- **The pharmacist** — frightened of the delivery company
- **Dispatch** — patient, dry, happy to repeat a detail

## Deaths

- Bud warns Dana before entering the warehouse alone. Ignoring him can end the case.
- Missing evidence is something to go back for; paperwork can be corrected.

content.thinking: I should also check logic 255 briefly, since death might reference f202.

The death message "You have died." fits a case-closing tone for a police game, editable later. I'm sketching the world layout: the Precinct Front Desk with Prakash, the board, and Bud, connecting to the Records Office and Main Street, while Main Street has a delivery driver and van, with exits back toward the precinct.

From Main Street, I'm branching to the pharmacy (with a pharmacist, broken window, and bottle evidence) and Pier Road Warehouse (with the suspect and Bud's warning), both looping back to Main Street. I'm setting up quest flags for tracking progress — assignment received, driver checked, pharmacy documented, warehouse connected, arrest made, and case filed — each with point values, and planning inventory items like badge, radio, camera, evidence bottle, ledger copy, and incident report, being careful about how item 0 behaves in the interpreter. I'm placing Prakash at the front desk as the opening scene, deciding where Bud should be positioned relative to the street.

Room 1 will have Prakash giving the assignment, a bulletin board, and a blinking radio, plus a camera that needs to be signed out from the equipment locker before it can be used at the pharmacy — Prakash won't let Reyes through the exits without the assignment flag set first. I'm also thinking ahead about how the final report-filing needs to loop back to this same room later once the other locations are built out.

For filing, I want Prakash to check for the completed set of evidence flags — driver, pharmacy, connected, arrest — and if anything's missing, he tells the player exactly what still needs doing rather than just failing silently. If everything checks out, I'm considering a little gag where there are two trays on the desk, an IN tray and a decoy, so the player has to notice which one is correct before successfully filing the report for the win.

I'm now sketching out the room layout for the precinct interior — dimensions, wall coloring, lighting — and planning which views I'll need (Dana, Prakash, the radio, the camera prop) along with reserving flag and variable bindings so later rooms can just set flags without redoing this setup.

Ego walks in front of the desk with baseline over 100, so the desk needs to occlude Prakash visually. I'm setting up priority bands by baseline row so the desk (priority 9) draws above Prakash (priority 8 at baseline 88), keeping the occlusion logic consistent even though the ego itself can never actually stand behind the desk.

For exits, I'm thinking through the room layout: a doorway on the left leading to the records hallway, with the left edge acting as a classic edge-exit to room 2, and the bottom edge implicitly representing the street door player came in through. I'm now considering whether to place another visible doorway on the right side wall instead.

I won't handle bottom edge collision, ego just stops there. For interactive objects: a blinking radio unit near the desk animates with two cels, dispatch radio in room 1 gives hints, and a camera sits in a locker that Prakash tells the player to sign out after assignment—once taken it's hidden and restored via a has(camera) flag. There's also a board that can be read for more info.

For the case itself: the pharmacy break-in happened overnight at Hale's Pharmacy, 14 Main Street, and delivery driver Rick Mendez claims he arrived at 6 AM to find the window already broken. But the dispatch log in room 2 shows his van was signed out at 1:30 AM, contradicting his story—confronting him with the log makes him admit he was actually there at 2 AM running off-the-books deliveries for his boss at the Quayside warehouse on Pier Road.

For scoring, checking the driver's story against the log discrepancy earns 25 points, photographing the pharmacy window and collecting the dropped pill bottle (which has a lot number) earns 30 points, and connecting the records ledger and the witness account to the warehouse earns 40 points. The pharmacist, frightened of the delivery company, reveals that Quayside's supplier deliveries have been short-counted with matching lot numbers, tying into the ledger clerk's records in room 2.

At the warehouse, entering alone without calling for backup gets Bud killed, so I need to radio for backup first before arresting the suspect (requiring the connected flag) for 60 points, then return to file the report. Bud shows up both on the street by the patrol car and again at the warehouse, so I'm now working out flag bindings like the assignment flag and camera usage flag.

I'm laying out the remaining flags for driver confirmation, pharmacy completion, connection, arrest, filing, and board reading, plus a variable tracking the radio blink cycle, and mapping out inventory slots for the badge, radio, camera, dispatch log, pill bottle, and driver statement while skipping handcuffs for now. With these bindings reserved, I'll move on to writing the world logic alongside them.

content.thinking:
I'm sketching Dana's design at roughly 8 wide by 30 tall, working out the color palette—navy uniform, black cap brim, medium brown skin tone, black hair, and details like the belt buckle and badge—before laying out a right-facing profile view at 7 wide by 30 tall.

Working row by row now: the cap silhouette, head with skin and hair, then the navy torso with badge and belt buckle placement, adjusting the pixel grid at each row to get the profile shape right.

Still designing walking frames...

Still mapping out the sprite grid...

Now I'm planning the back-view sprite without a face, then shifting to designing Prakash's figure behind the desk—giving him grey hair and a mustache while keeping him full-bodied though mostly hidden.

Still writing sprite rows...

Adding a blinking green light for the radio's second cel, then sketching a small camera sprite to place on a shelf. Now I'm planning the room layout: a light gray back wall with a green wainscot band, a ceiling strip, and a dark gray floor for contrast against the navy Dana character.

Settling on ceiling gray, green walls, brown wainscot, and a light gray linoleum floor for good contrast with both navy characters. I'm now placing details—a bulletin board with a brown cork frame and white paper rectangles on the wall, plus a tall gray equipment locker standing nearby.

I'm working out a shelf unit against the wall with a brown frame and a dark open cubby where a small camera object sits, then moving to the desk: a long counter with a brown front face and figuring out the right top surface color to distinguish it from the floor.

Behind the desk, I'm placing Prakash so his upper body shows above the desk edge while his lower body is occluded, using a priority setting so the desk visually covers his legs correctly against the wall and floor layers. I'm also adding a couple of small trays on the desk surface for a labeling gag, sized to sit just above the desk top line.

Now I'm laying out the room's exits: a dark corridor opening on the left edge of the floor suggesting a hallway west, and glass double doors on the right wall as the exit point, plus marking the desk's footprint as a barrier to block movement through it.

For the desk occlusion, I'm weighing whether I actually need priority zero blocking there since the ego never walks behind the desk — that only matters for Prakash's sprite. I'm considering how AGI's priority screen values would interact with a sprite's priority when drawing him behind the desk.

Instead I'll add invisible priority-0 barrier lines just outside the desk footprint (vertical edges at x74 and x138 from y76-106, plus a horizontal line at y106) on floor pixels so they stay invisible while still blocking the ego from walking into the desk area. Left locker against the wall above the horizon shouldn't need separate blocking.

Checking priorities: ego baseline at 76 gets priority 7, drawn over the wall's priority 4, so standing near it looks correct, and the board is similarly drawn behind the ego. I don't think I need an extra barrier at the bottom floor edge since the ego just naturally stops there.

For spawn and exits, Dana starts at x60,y130, and the left/right edges act as exits that require an assignment first -- otherwise Prakash calls the ego back with a line about needing an assignment before leaving.

For repositioning ego when unassigned, I'll grab the current position and use it to snap the ego back to the edge, then reset the movement variable manually. Now I'm drafting the opening message for the first entry, setting the scene at 7:58 AM with Sergeant Prakash.

I'm writing out the front desk description—Prakash behind the counter, the bulletin board, records hallway west, and doors leading east to Main Street—along with his dialogue branches: the initial briefing about the pharmacy break-in and painkiller theft, then his instructions to check the delivery driver's story, review dispatch logs in records, and sign out a camera before heading out, which sets a flag once delivered.

I'm also outlining the sequence of reminders Prakash gives depending on progress—comparing the driver's story to the dispatch log, photographing the pharmacy, checking the Quayside ledger, heading to Pier Road with backup, and eventually filing the report before being told to go home. The bulletin board itself lists the case details: Hale's Pharmacy break-in, the driver's report time, the missing painkillers, and the assigned officers.

Looking around the desk, I note the two labeled trays, some flavor text about Prakash's decades on the job and his skepticism toward paperwork, and the department camera on the equipment shelf. Taking the camera only works if I've actually been assigned a task first—otherwise Prakash turns me away for not having an assignment yet.

For the wall radio, calling dispatch gives a reminder of case details, while trying to call backup while already at the station gets a joke response pointing out I'm literally standing in the police station. Showing or examining my badge gets some flavor confirming Prakash issued it Monday, and photographing without a camera or with nothing worth capturing both give dismissive responses. Bud, meanwhile, is out at the patrol car on Main Street rather than in the building.

Filing the report is gated behind completing each piece of evidence -- I need the driver's story checked against dispatch logs, pharmacy photos, the Pier Road link, and an arrest with backup before it's complete. Once everything's in place, Prakash catches me putting it in the wrong tray, reads through the finished report, praises the solid case, tells me it's a good first week, and sends me home -- ending the shift.

Now I'm mapping out the vocabulary the parser needs to recognize: verbs like look, talk, read, take, show, check, radio/call, photograph, and nouns covering all the key objects and people -- badge, driver, pharmacy, bottle, ledger, warehouse, suspect, report, Prakash, board, camera, tray, desk, locker, dispatch, backup, partner, file, door, records, and case-related terms, making sure synonyms like "radio" and "call" map to the same underlying action.

I'm deciding whether "check" should be treated as its own separate word or folded into the look/examine group, and I'm leaning toward keeping them grouped together for simplicity while still allowing room-specific phrases like "check board" or "check ledger" to work, and small filler words like "a," "the," "to," "at," and "in" get ignored during parsing.

I still need to plan verb groups for take/grab, show/give, file/submit, photograph/snap, and talk/ask/tell, plus register key nouns like the sergeant's name, story, log, statement, and location objects so later rooms can reference them. I also want to make sure the "inventory" command is handled globally by adding a said("inventory") check in the base logic before falling through to other handlers, so pressing that shows player status regardless of room.
